h1: How winemakers blend wine across varieties and barrels
title: How Winemakers Blend Wine | Craft Beer School
desc: How winemakers blend wine across grape varieties, vineyard lots and barrels, why they do it and how a blending trial works.
teaser: Most wines you drink are blends, even the ones with one grape on the label.
standfirst: Blending is where a winemaker turns a cellar full of separate lots into one wine with a clear identity. Here is why it is done, what gets blended and how the decisions are made at the tasting bench.
sections:
When people hear "blend" they think of a mix of grapes, like the Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot wines of Bordeaux. That is one kind. In practice almost every wine is a blend of something.

  • Varieties. Different grapes combined for balance. Classic examples are Bordeaux reds and the Grenache, Shiraz and Mourvèdre blends of the southern Rhône.
  • Vineyard lots. Grapes from different blocks, slopes or growers. One block may give colour and another fresh acidity.
  • Barrels and tanks. The same wine aged in different barrels tastes different. New oak, older oak and steel tanks each contribute something.
  • Vintages. Non-vintage Champagne and many sparkling wines blend reserve wine from earlier years to keep a house style consistent.

A wine labelled with one grape can still contain some of another. Many countries allow a varietal label if the wine contains a minimum share of that grape, such as 85% under EU rules.

Blending solves problems and builds something better than the parts.

  • Balance. A wine with great fruit but little acid can be lifted by a fresher lot.
  • Complexity. Two good wines with different strengths can make a more interesting third.
  • Consistency. A brand that sells every year needs to taste much the same every year, even when the weather changes.
  • Volume. A small lot that is excellent but too small to bottle alone can lift a larger blend.

Whisky blenders work in a very similar way, as our guide to how whisky blenders keep brands consistent shows.

The classic Bordeaux blend shows the logic well. Cabernet Sauvignon brings structure, firm tannin and blackcurrant. Merlot fills the middle with softer, plummy fruit. Cabernet Franc adds perfume and freshness. Petit Verdot, used in small amounts, deepens colour and spice.

White blends follow the same idea. Sémillon gives body and texture while Sauvignon Blanc adds bright acidity and aroma. Our grape varieties guide describes what each common grape tastes like on its own.

Blending decisions are made at a bench, not in a tank. A typical trial looks like this.

  1. Taste each lot on its own and write notes on its strengths and faults.
  2. Make small trial blends in measuring cylinders, using pipettes for accuracy. Proportions are recorded exactly, for example 60% lot A, 30% lot B and 10% lot C.
  3. Taste the trials blind against each other, ideally with more than one person.
  4. Narrow down, adjust by a few per cent and taste again.
  5. Check the chosen blend in the lab for alcohol, acidity, pH, residual sugar and free sulphur dioxide.
  6. Scale up in the cellar, mix thoroughly and taste the tank against the bench sample.

A few per cent of a strongly flavoured lot can change a blend a great deal. That is why trials are measured in millilitres and recorded precisely.

Some winemakers blend early, sometimes even fermenting different grapes together, which is called co-fermentation. Others keep every lot separate through ageing and blend only months later, when they know how each one has developed. Late blending gives more control. Early blending can give a more integrated wine and saves tank space.

After blending, the wine usually rests for a few weeks so the components settle together before bottling. Our guide to how wine is made shows where blending sits in the whole process.

Indian wineries blend for the same reasons as anywhere else. Fruit from different growers and regions can vary a lot, since Indian vineyards are often small and spread out. Blending lots from several growers helps a brand stay consistent from year to year.

Heat also plays a part. A short ripening window can leave one lot ripe and soft while another stays sharper. Blending them can give a better balanced wine than either alone. Some Indian wineries blend Shiraz with Cabernet Sauvignon, or Sauvignon Blanc with Chenin Blanc, to balance body and freshness.

Blending is a skill built on tasting, record keeping and a clear idea of what the finished wine should be. It is learnt the same way a brewer learns recipe design, by understanding what each part brings before putting them together.
faqs: Is a blended wine lower quality than a single-variety wine?
No. Many of the world's most famous wines are blends, including classic Bordeaux and Champagne. Blending is a quality tool, not a shortcut.
Can a wine labelled with one grape contain others?
Often yes. Many countries allow a varietal label if the wine contains a minimum share of that grape, for example 85% under EU rules.
Why do sparkling wines blend vintages?
To keep a consistent house style. Reserve wines from earlier years smooth out the differences between harvests.
